title: Read any pattern, check your gauge and resize with confidence

say: Read any pattern, check your gauge, and resize with confidence.
This is the video for module one of Advanced Knitting and Crochet.
Read the pattern once, start to finish, before you cast on or chain.
Check the materials: can you get this yarn, and do you have the needle or hook? Then the gauge. Which stitch is it measured in?

panel.heading: Scan six sections, in this order
items: Materials: yarn, needle or hook, notions
Gauge: stitches and rows in 10 cm

say: Choose your size by finished measurement, not by the letter. Then circle every number for your size through the whole pattern, so you never read the wrong one mid-row.

panel.heading: Scan six sections, in this order
items: Materials: yarn, needle or hook, notions
Gauge: stitches and rows in 10 cm

say: Check the abbreviations, then the instructions. A stitch count at the end of a row, like 48 stitches, is your checkpoint. Count after every shaping row. Finally, read the finishing notes.

panel.heading: Scan six sections, in this order
items: Materials: yarn, needle or hook, notions
Gauge: stitches and rows in 10 cm

say: Here is the mistake to avoid. The same name means different stitches. A US single crochet is a UK double crochet.
If you follow a US pattern with UK stitches, every stitch is one step too tall, and the piece grows longer and wider than planned.

panel.heading: US and UK crochet terms differ

say: Look for clues. US patterns use sc and hdc. UK patterns use htr, and say tension and miss instead of gauge and skip.

panel.heading: US and UK crochet terms differ

say: On a chart, each square is one stitch, and the key explains each symbol. Find row 1. It is at the bottom, because fabric grows upward.

panel.heading: One square is one stitch
items: Flat: right-side rows right to left
Flat: wrong-side rows left to right
In the round: every row right to left
Keep a ruler above your working row
panel.rule: Row 1 is at the bottom, because fabric grows upward.

say: For flat knitting, read right-side rows from right to left, and wrong-side rows from left to right.

say: Gauge, called tension in UK patterns, is how many stitches and rows fit into 10 cm. Two women with the same yarn and needles can get different gauge.
Use the project yarn, and make the swatch about 15 cm square, because edges are always uneven.

panel.heading: Make a swatch you can trust
items: Same yarn, suggested needle or hook
Work the stitch the gauge names

say: Work the stitch the gauge line names. Then block it the way you will wash the finished item: soak, press out water in a towel, and dry it flat.

panel.heading: Make a swatch you can trust
items: Same yarn, suggested needle or hook
Work the stitch the gauge names
panel.rule: Swatch in the stitch the gauge line names, then wash it.

say: Measure across 15 cm and divide. Half a stitch per centimetre changes the size a lot.

panel.heading: Make a swatch you can trust
items: Same yarn, suggested needle or hook
Work the stitch the gauge names
panel.rule: Swatch in the stitch the gauge line names, then wash it.

say: For example, Funke in Ibadan is making a cotton jumper. The pattern gauge is 22 stitches to 10 cm on 4 mm needles, and the front is 110 stitches.
Her washed swatch has 30 stitches in 15 cm. That is 2.0 stitches per cm, or 20 per 10 cm.
The pattern front would be 110 divided by 2.2, which is 50 cm. Hers would be 55 cm. Front and back together, the jumper would be 10 cm too big around.
Her fabric is looser, so she goes down to 3.5 mm needles. The new swatch counts 33 stitches in 15 cm, exactly 22 per 10 cm. One evening of swatching saved the whole jumper.
When the sizes do not fit the body, you can resize. Start from the finished measurement you want, including ease, not the body measurement.
Stitches equal target width in centimetres times stitches per centimetre.

cards.d: Target width in cm x stitches per cm. Stitches per cm is your gauge divided by 10.
Target length in cm x rows per cm. Add length in plain sections, not in the shaping.
Yarn rises with stitches: 20% wider needs about 20% more yarn. Buy one dye lot.

say: Rows equal target length times rows per centimetre. Add length in the plain section below the armhole.

cards.d: Target width in cm x stitches per cm. Stitches per cm is your gauge divided by 10.
Target length in cm x rows per cm. Add length in plain sections, not in the shaping.
Yarn rises with stitches: 20% wider needs about 20% more yarn. Buy one dye lot.

say: And yarn rises with the stitches. Buy the extra from the same dye lot.

cards.d: Target width in cm x stitches per cm. Stitches per cm is your gauge divided by 10.
Target length in cm x rows per cm. Add length in plain sections, not in the shaping.
Yarn rises with stitches: 20% wider needs about 20% more yarn. Buy one dye lot.

say: For example, Grace in Jos needs a cardigan back of about 56 cm. At 2 stitches per cm, that is 112 stitches. But her cable rib is a multiple of 6 plus 2.
112 minus 2 is 110, and 110 does not divide by 6. So 112 will break the pattern.
The nearest counts that fit are 110 or 116. She chooses 110 stitches, a back of 55 cm, which still gives about 8 cm of ease.
Never add one or two stitches in the middle of a repeat. Round to a count that fits, then recheck the width.

panel.heading: Grace's cardigan: fit the repeat
panel.rule: Round to a count that fits the repeat, then recheck the width.

say: To remember. Scan the six sections every time. Know if your crochet terms are US or UK. Swatch 15 cm and wash it before measuring. Width is stitches divided by stitches per centimetre. And round to fit the repeat, then recheck the width.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Scan the six sections every time

Round to fit the repeat, recheck width
